title: Avoid scams and fraud during Open Enrollment - Fox 59

Avoid scams and fraud during open enrollment | Fox 59 
 Fox 59 
 Avoid scams and fraud during open enrollment
 Zach Myers 
 1 hour ago 
 FILE - A Medicare Advantage PPO card rests on top of a Medicare card in Portland, Ore., June 10, 2024. (AP Photo/Jenny Kane, File) 
 WXIN/WTTV — While health insurance scams happen all year, they really pick up during open enrollment season.
 According to experts, stolen medical records can be 10 to 50 times more valuable than a stolen credit card number when sold on the dark web. That’s why medical identity fraud is a constant threat, especially during the last few months of the year.  
 Open enrollment for Medicare is happening now and the Federal Trade Commission is sharing some reminders about staying safe when searching for information or a new plan.
 If you’re doing an online search, the FTC says it’s important to remember you can’t always trust “paid” or “sponsored” results that appear first. Crooks sometimes pay to put their websites at the top of search results and those links can take you to bogus, copycat websites. Instead, the FTC says, you should scroll past those “sponsored” links and look for the .gov ending on the address.
 The safest method is to type Medicare.gov or Healthcare.gov  directly into your web address bar.  From there, you can compare health insurance plans, check your coverage, or see if you qualify for savings. You can also get help and information through the State Health Insurance Assistance Program (SHIP) or the local Senior Medical Patrol. 
 According to Trendlife, there are several scams that tend to pick up this time of year. One to watch for is a fake agent call, where here somebody claims to represent Medicare and says you qualify for a better plan.  
 Another scam involves a new Medicare card request, where somebody calls and says Medicare is issuing new cards and they need you to verify your Medicare number or pay a fee. You should also watch for calls or texts about “important medical notices,” where somebody impersonates the government and tries to get you on the line with a scammer.
 The most important thing to remember is that you should never give out any medical or otherwise sensitive information to someone who contacted you unexpectedly. If you encounter a scammer, you can report them to the FTC at ReportFraud.ftc.gov .
